newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Imperilled deals await new U.S. foreign policy team.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Imperilled deals await new U.S. foreign policy team.

text.p: Warren Christopher, said by his aides to have achieved more than any other recent U.S. secretary of state, leaves his successor Madeleine Albright a legacy of deals that are threatening to crumble.

From Bosnia to the Middle East to North Korea, the landmark international agreements of the first Clinton administration are in difficulties and will require major efforts in the coming year to shore them up.

Albright, Washington's U.N. ambassador who will move to the state department on January 20, also faces a looming confrontation with Russia over NATO expansion and the thorny task of managing ties with the unpredictable rulers of China.

State department officials say Christopher, in a sign-off report to President Bill Clinton, saw global problems like population, climate change, drugs and food security as the main challenges ahead. He himself said this week that "these will be perhaps the key issues as we turn to a new century".
PEACE DEALS UNDER THREAT
But, as usual, urgent crises in world trouble spots seem likely to push those issues down Albright's agenda.

Christopher's staff maintain that "more was done on his watch" than in any other four-year period for decades. They cite the Dayton agreement on Bosnia, the Oslo Middle East peace accords and deals on North Korea and Haiti.
But events in 1996 conspired to put the future of these agreements into question.

In the Middle East, the election of a right-wing Likud government in Israel has been followed by a serious loss of confidence between the Israelis and their Palestinian negotiating partners, analysts say. An Israeli-Syrian peace deal, seen as likely a year ago, has receded over the horizon.

Despite growing U.S. irritation over the slow pace of Israeli-Palestinian negotiations and Israel's settlements policy, Washington has maintained its line that it is up to the parties themselves to resolve their difficulties.
NEW FOCUS ON EUROPE
Many Arab officials fear that unless the next U.S. administration takes a more hands-on approach to push the negotiations ahead, violence could erupt again in the region.

But analysts suspect that the attention of the Czech-born Albright and her deputy, Russia expert Strobe Talbott, will focus more on Europe, especially Bosnia, where thousands of U.S. troops will remain in an international peace force.

Although the November 1995 Dayton accords stopped the war in Bosnia, fears of renewed fighting have compelled NATO to prepare a slimmed down force to remain there for 18 months after the December 20 expiry of the original peacekeeping force's mandate.

A multi-ethnic Bosnian government is struggling into life but its long-term survival still seems threatened by persistent racial hatreds, the inability of refugees to return home and the failure so far to arrest indicted war criminals.

In North Korea, a breakthrough 1994 pact with the United States to halt Pyongyang's nuclear programme has been stalled by an incident last September in which a North Korean submarine landed armed commandos on a South Korean beach.
U.S. officials are trying to hammer out a deal with the North Koreans whereby Pyongyang would express regret over the incident, clearing the way for progress on other fronts.
RUSSIAN FEAR OF NATO

U.S. relations with Russia, which Washington has managed to keep on an even keel despite the turbulent course of events in Moscow, look headed for trouble when NATO announces in July which East European states it will take in as new members.

Talbott's close rapport with the Russian leadership will be stretched to the limit to persuade Moscow that its ties to the West outweigh the security threat it sees from the absorption of its former allies into NATO.
With China, Albright inherits slightly improved relations after some two years of tensions over Taiwan, arms proliferation, trade and human rights.

But the improvement has been bought at the cost of downgrading human rights on the U.S. agenda and a see-no-evil policy on China's alleged nuclear and missile sales to Pakistan and Iran that may bode future problems with Congress.
VOTERS AND CONGRESS DON'T CARE

Albright takes over at a time of almost unprecedented public and Congressional indifference to foreign affairs and little sign that Clinton is going to shift his primary focus away from domestic issues.

At one televised debate in the presidential election campaign between Clinton and challenger Bob Dole in October, the studio audience asked only one foreign policy question. The question, which had to be solicited by the moderator, was on U.S. trade problems with Japan.

Repeated appeals by Christopher and his lieutenants were unable to stem the steady decline in budget allocations for the state department, forcing Christopher to recommend closure of some 30 U.S. embassies and consulates during his tenure.
Foreign policy experts in the Republican-led Congress said the state department had "failed to make the case" for evading budget cuts and that they looked to Albright to do better.
